meaning: Performing rights organization. A group (ASCAP and BMI are the big U.S. ones) that collects money for songwriters when their songs are played on streaming services, radio, TV and live venues.

A unique ID number given to a songwriter or publisher when they join a PRO. You may also see it called a CAE number. It identifies you in royalty systems, so keep it handy for split sheets and The MLC.

International Standard Recording Code. A unique code for one specific recording, like a barcode for that track. Your distributor usually creates it for you, and the same recording always keeps the same ISRC.
Universal Product Code. A barcode number for a whole release (a single, EP or album). Your distributor assigns it when you upload.

International Standard Musical Work Code. A unique code for the song itself (the melody and lyrics), not for any one recording of it. It is assigned after the song is registered with a collection organization.
Digital service provider: a streaming or download service such as Spotify, Apple Music or Amazon Music.
The Mechanical Licensing Collective. A U.S. organization that collects digital mechanical royalties from streaming services and pays them to songwriters and publishers.
Money paid to songwriters and publishers for the copies of a song that are made when it is streamed or downloaded. In the U.S., The MLC collects the digital kind.
Royalties for a recording being played on digital radio and similar services, paid to the recording's owner and performers. In the U.S., SoundExchange collects them.
The finished recording itself, the audio file. Whoever owns the master owns the recording.
The song itself: the melody and lyrics, separate from any recording of it. Songwriters (and their publishers) own it, and it earns its own royalties.
The information that travels with your music: titles, artist names, songwriter and producer credits, release date and so on. Mistakes in it can send royalties to the wrong place.
Electronic press kit. One page or file with your bio, photos, music links and contact details that you can send to bookers, bloggers and playlist curators.
Call to action: the one thing you want people to do when they see your post, like pre-saving or listening to the new song.
A link that lets fans save your upcoming song to their library before it is out, so it is already there on release day.
The company that delivers your finished music to streaming services and collects the recording earnings for you.
Money a label pays up front that is later deducted from your royalties (see recoupment).
When a label has paid costs or an advance, it keeps your royalties until it earns that money back. Until then you may be paid nothing.
Losses on one release or cost can be charged against what you earn from others, so the amount you need to earn back keeps growing.
A clause that gives you your rights back after a set time, or if the label stops releasing your music.
A short signed agreement of who owns what share of a song's recording and of the song itself.
A license to use your music in a video, film, show or ad. It earns its own fee.
